senses.gloss:
1. Sic denotes the ‘border’ of a garment. The Rigveda refers to a son clutching the hem of his father's robe to attract his attention, and to a mother's covering her son with the edge of her garment. The word also occurs later.
Foot notes iii. 53, 2.
x. 18, 11.
Av. xiv. 2, 51; Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, iii. 2, 1, 18.

2. Sic denotes, in the dual, the ‘wings’ of an army, or, in the plural, the ‘lines.’
2) Av. xi. 9, 18; 10, 20.
Cf. Pischel, Vedische Studien, 2, 65; Geldner, ibid., 3, 31.
Foot notes Rv. x. 75, 4.
3. Sic seems in one passage of the Rigveda (i. 95, 7), where it is used in the dual, to denote the ‘horizon’ (meaning literally the ‘two borders’; i.e., of heaven and of earth).

Sīcāpū in the list of victims at the aśvamedha (‘horse sacrifice’) in the yajurveda seems to denote a kind of bird.
Foot notes Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 19, 6; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 25. Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 94.
